report:
Likely difference: Model B is more “news/media headline and caption” biased.

Why I think this
- Strong first-token effect: The difference norm is overwhelmingly concentrated at position 0 across many layers (especially L25 p0 = 322), consistent with a start-of-document/title/lede prior.
- Headline/caption lexicon shows up repeatedly in the logit-lens tops:
  - Explicit “headline” tokens: headline, headlines.
  - Proper names and surname particles common in news: Driver, Vincent, Hunter, Manny, Royals; von/van/de/sur; diacritics (é), foreign words (på, jeg).
  - News/disaster terms: tragic, tragedy, victims, refugees, hurricane, shocked, refused, forced, blitz, worst.
  - Entertainment/culture adjectives typical of captions/listicles: iconic, vivid, colorful, timeless, loud, vibrant, lush, furry, melodic; rocker, podcast, UFO.
  - Listicle/title scaffolding: numbers (6,8,7,9,5), All/all, newlines, Coming/Buy/Buying/Currently/Do/Once.
- This cluster is especially strong in deeper layers at positions 2–4 (e.g., “iconic/vivid/colorful/timeless/tragic” dominate across L21–L25), which looks like a style/content prior rather than a single topic word.

Caveats
- There are some how-to/optimization tokens (check, optimize, prevent, recommendations), but the dominant, repeated pattern is news/caption/headline style and proper-noun-heavy text.
- Patchscope readouts weren’t available here, so the conclusion rests on norms and logit-lens patterns.

Bottom line: Compared to A, B appears more inclined toward producing newsy, headline/caption-like continuations with proper names and vivid/tragic descriptive adjectives, especially influencing the very first token and propagating into early continuation tokens.
